title: Gangster No. 1
full_review:
An ambitious young thug claws his way up the 1960s London gangland hierarchy in the sick drama "Gangster No. 1" (IFC Films).

Paul Bettany has chosen a slick, demented role far from his charming Geoffrey Chaucer character in "A Knight's Tale" or the devoted but imaginary best friend of John Nash in "A Beautiful Mind." The lanky, strawberry-blond actor plays the main character in director Paul McGuigan's British film, which -- despite its stylish presentation -- is mired in egregious, brutal violence that becomes increasingly unpalatable.

Bettany's character is referred to simply as Gangster, seemingly an attempt to make both him and the violence generic. Malcolm McDowell plays the now-aging Gangster, who recalls his past glory days in voiceover, regaling the audience with how Gangster made it to his present, lofty position among the gangland leaders of London.

The story itself is rather slim as it charts the rise and fall of Gangster's success in the mob business. The main interest is Bettany's performance and the transformation his character undergoes. Plucked off the streets by established gangland leader Freddie Mays (David Thewlis), Gangster impresses the mobster with his fearless attitude and is placed on the payroll. As the camera lingers over Freddie's sharp double-breasted mohair suits, glossy Italian leather shoes and initialed ruby and pearl tie pin, the viewer is lead to become just as intoxicated as Gangster does with the gang leader's ultra-cool flamboyance. More than just power, Freddie has class and sophistication to spare. And Gangster admires Freddie and all he possesses with a frightening intensity.

"Gangster No. 1" is a disturbing tale of one man's ruthless ambition, envy and betrayal. It is not enough for Gangster to be near Freddie; he wants to be Freddie. This desire gnaws at his very soul as Gangster goes from street thug to a "respected" member of Freddie's family. But what Gangster has is not enough, and his obsession builds to psychosis. And when Freddie's life becomes complete with the addition of Karen (Saffron Burrows), a singer who chooses Freddie over Gangster, Gangster's jealousy turns into rage, setting in motion his devious plan to topple Freddie.

The last reel of the film leaps from the 1960s to the present time, when Gangster (McDowell) is a more successful mobster than Freddie ever dreamed of being. But instead of feeling happiness or fulfillment, Gangster has grown more bitter and envious with each year. All he possesses, all his power and money, have failed to gain him the one thing that has seemingly eluded him: love.

However, though this sentiment may seem mushy, there is not a single sugar-coated moment in the film. Take for example the night young Gangster takes out Freddie's main adversary, Lenny (Jamie Foreman). Calmly and deliberately, Gangster strips to his underclothes, to avoid soiling them, before hacking the wounded Lenny to pieces. The bloody scene is all the more brazenly brutal for what it doesn't show. The audience sees Gangster's hand raised defiantly before it smashes down straight at the camera lens as if it were Lenny's poor face. With blood splattered all over his body, Gangster sits smoking a cigarette in an armchair after Lenny is dead, sedately assessing his work. And there are other similar scenes, one involving golf clubs as weapons used to bludgeon body parts and to crack bones, that are just as repugnant.

Bettany plays Gangster with a quiet, creepy intensity that catapults the grisly violence to a higher level. It is unnerving to watch Bettany's face twist as his pale smile curls into a vicious snarl -� and all the while McDowell's steady yet piercing voice narrates the story. Both Bettany and McDowell never let up their intensity. Their cold impenetrable eyes reveal the storm of madness swirling inside Gangster. But while Bettany's performance is one of fierce control, McDowell disappoints by taking the easier route in his pivotal final scenes by stomping about and yelling.

Director McGuigan has created a sleek, swaggering film intended to slowly strip away the glamour of the gangster lifestyle. Yet "Gangster No. 1" loses this central element by focusing on the seamier, barbaric side of a mobster mentality devoid of any moral code. Instead, the film becomes drenched in inescapable savagery that each passing minute becomes more repellent than the next.

Due to much savage, graphic violence, full frontal nudity, brief drug use and constant rough language with some profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
(
2002
)
